lead: IPv4 gives each interface a 32-bit address, and its header carries a checksum that every router must check. IPv6 replaces this with 128-bit addresses and one fixed 40-byte base header. The larger address space covers phones, servers, sensors and home routers without address sharing. The simpler header lets routers forward packets faster. You meet IPv6 in mobile data, cloud networks and broadband. Because IPv4 still runs, the move uses dual stack, tunnelling and translation.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for IPv4 address parts and Chapter 4.3 for IPv4 header fields, MTU and fragmentation.

blocks.text: An IPv6 address is 128 bits. It is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, separated by colons. Each hex digit is 4 bits; four hex digits are 16 bits; eight groups give 128 bits. Hex digits run 0–9 and a–f.

blocks.where: Each group has four hexadecimal digits; one hexadecimal digit carries 4 bits.

blocks.text: Two compression rules keep text short. Drop leading zeros inside a group: 0db8 becomes db8. Replace one longest run of all-zero groups by ::, and use :: at most once. Thus 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 becomes 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.

The /n suffix gives the prefix length, as in IPv4. A /64 LAN prefix fixes the first 64 bits (four groups) and leaves 64 bits for hosts. SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets a host build its own interface identifier from the /64 prefix and a router advertisement, so no DHCP server is needed.
Address types are unicast (one interface), multicast (a group) and anycast (nearest member of a group). IPv6 has no broadcast; multicast does that job.

Every IPv6 base header is 40 bytes. The figure lists its fields in order. Version is 4 bits and holds 6. Traffic class is 8 bits for priority. Flow label is 20 bits to mark packets that need the same treatment. Payload length is 16 bits and counts bytes after the header. Next header is 8 bits and names the next header, such as TCP or an extension header. Hop limit is 8 bits and is decreased by each router. Source and destination addresses are 128 bits each.

Compared with IPv4, there is no header checksum. Transport and link layers already check errors, so routers do not recompute a checksum. Routers also do not fragment; a source that sends a large packet must learn the path MTU and fragment itself. Optional functions move into extension headers, chained by the next header field.
Dual stack means a host or router runs IPv4 and IPv6 together. It has both address types and chooses the version from the destination address or DNS answer.

Tunnelling carries an IPv6 packet inside an IPv4 packet across a region that only forwards IPv4. The tunnel ends at a dual-stack router, which removes the IPv4 outer header. IPv6-in-IPv4 uses IP protocol number 41.
Translation rewrites headers and addresses between versions. NAT64 lets an IPv6-only host reach an IPv4 server; details are in Chapter 4.5.
Real networks mix these. A mobile operator may run IPv6 with dual stack at the edge; an enterprise may tunnel between sites; a data centre may translate at the border.

figure.caption: Groups 3, 4 and 5 are the longest run of all-zero groups, so one :: replaces them and gives 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329. The /64 LAN prefix keeps only the first four groups: 2001:db8:0:0::/64.

examples.question: Expand and compress the IPv6 address 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329. State the number of groups, the number of zero groups replaced by ::, and the /64 LAN prefix. Name one transition method.
steps: Split into 8 groups: 2001 | 0db8 | 0000 | 0000 | 0000 | ff00 | 0042 | 8329. Count = 8 groups.
Remove leading zeros in each group: 2001 | db8 | 0 | 0 | 0 | ff00 | 42 | 8329.
Find the longest run of all-zero groups: groups 3, 4 and 5, length 3. Replace that run with one ::. Compressed form: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329.
A /64 prefix uses the first 64 bits = first 4 groups. First four groups are 2001, db8, 0 and 0. Write them and trailing zero groups as ::, giving 2001:db8:0:0::/64.
Transition method: dual stack. A host keeps IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and selects the version by destination.
examples.answer: The address has 8 groups, 3 consecutive zero groups are compressed by one ::, and the /64 LAN prefix is 2001:db8:0:0::/64; use dual stack.
examples.check:
addr = '2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329'
groups = addr.split(':')
n_groups = len(groups)
runs = []
i = 0
while i < len(groups):
    if groups[i] == '0000':
        j = i
        while j < len(groups) and groups[j] == '0000':
            j += 1
        runs.append(j - i)
        i = j
    else:
        i += 1
zero_run = max(runs) if runs else 0
prefix_len = 64
print(n_groups)
print(zero_run)
print(prefix_len)

traps: Using :: twice in one address makes it ambiguous; only one zero run may be compressed.
Calling the IPv6 header variable length: the base header is fixed at 40 bytes; extension headers add length after it.
Forgetting that hop limit does the job of IPv4 TTL; there is no TTL field in IPv6.
Mixing unicast, multicast and anycast: anycast delivers to one nearest member, multicast to all members of a group.
Writing a /64 prefix with host bits left set; a prefix ends at bit 64 and is written as ...::/64.

quiz.q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address, and how many hexadecimal groups are used to write it?
quiz.a: 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits.

quiz.q: Why does IPv6 drop the header checksum?
quiz.a: Transport and link layers detect errors; routers avoid recomputing a checksum on every hop.
Remove leading zeros: 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1. The longest zero run is groups 3–7, length 5, so replace it with one ::. Answer: 2001:db8::1.
First 64 bits are the first four groups: 2001:db8:abcd:1234::/64.

quiz.q: A router receives an IPv6 packet larger than the next link's MTU. What does the router do?
quiz.a: It drops the packet and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big to the source. The source fragments; IPv6 routers do not fragment.

quiz.q: State one difference between hop limit and IPv4 TTL.
quiz.a: Both limit hop count; IPv6 calls the field hop limit and each router decreases it by one. It is 8 bits.

quiz.q: Why is using :: twice in one address wrong? Give an example.
quiz.a: It gives two possible lengths for the zero run, so the address cannot be expanded uniquely. 2001::db8::1 could expand in more than one way.

quiz.q: Name the three common IPv4-to-IPv6 transition methods.

beyond: Not for the exam. IPv6 is the normal carrying protocol in many mobile and cloud networks, and extension headers are used for mobility, segment routing and security. Researchers study address scanning, transition security and IPv6 deployment measurement. Search next for SLAAC, NAT64, DHCPv6, IPv6 extension headers and 6LoWPAN.
